name: Palantir
summary: Candidates report a recruiter call, an online assessment or live technical screen, then an onsite of three or so rounds drawn from decomposition, learning, re-engineering (debugging), coding and system design, followed by a hiring manager call. Most rounds reserve time for behavioural and motivation questions.

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.what: Why Palantir, SWE versus forward deployed fit, and past projects you liked and disliked.

rounds.name: Online assessment (some candidates)
rounds.what: HackerRank with a coding problem, a SQL query and a REST API task.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.what: Data structures and algorithms framed as a product feature, plus behavioural questions.

rounds.name: Decomposition
rounds.what: Break a vague real-world problem into parts, agree on an approach, then sketch data and components.

rounds.name: Learning
rounds.what: Learn an unfamiliar API or concept in the interview and use it on tasks of rising difficulty.

rounds.name: Re-engineering
rounds.what: Debug and review an unfamiliar codebase whose output is wrong; watch for red herrings.

rounds.name: Onsite coding
rounds.what: An intentionally vague problem; clarify, then discuss caching, trade-offs and misuse.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.what: Standard system design with behavioural questions; permissions and audit come up.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.what: Revisits weak spots from the loop, motivation and team matching.

tips: Have a specific, sincere answer to why Palantir; it is asked in nearly every round.
Tie technical choices back to the end user and say how the solution could improve.
In decomposition, clarify data sources, users and constraints before designing.
In re-engineering, form hypotheses and test them instead of reading every line or rewriting.
In the learning round, ask questions and narrate how you are learning.
